explain.answer: Hydrogen bonds hold ice in an open lattice, so ice is less dense.

trick.text: Ice floats because hydrogen bonds hold it open.

steps: In ice, each water makes four **hydrogen bonds**.
Those bonds fix molecules in an open, hexagonal lattice.
The lattice leaves empty space between molecules.
In liquid, bonds break and reform, so molecules pack closer.
Same mass in more volume: ice is less dense and floats.

traps.A: Specific heat explains slow temperature change, not why ice floats.
traps.B: Cohesion explains surface tension. It does not open up the solid.
traps.C: Solvent power is about dissolving ions. It does not set the density of ice.
traps.E: Polar bonds turning toward ions describes dissolving, not the ice lattice.

check.q: Why does a lake not freeze solid from the bottom up?
check.a: Ice is less dense, floats, and insulates the water below.

explain.answer: Sugar, phosphate and base make a nucleotide, the monomer of nucleic acids.

trick.text: Sugar, phosphate, base: that is a nucleotide.

steps: List the parts: **five-carbon sugar**, phosphate, nitrogenous base.
Sugar plus phosphate plus base is one nucleotide.
Nucleotides link into DNA or RNA.
So the polymer is a nucleic acid.

traps.A: Polysaccharides are built from simple sugars only. No phosphate, no base.
traps.B: Lipids have no repeating monomer that carries a nitrogenous base.
traps.D: Proteins are built from amino acids, not sugar, phosphate and base.
traps.E: A glycoprotein is protein plus sugar. It has no nitrogenous bases.

check.q: Which sugar is in an RNA nucleotide?

explain.answer: Starch has α-1,4 links; cellulose has β-1,4 links our enzymes cannot cut.

trick.text: Alpha links we digest; beta links need microbes.

steps: Both polymers are chains of **D-glucose**.
Starch joins glucose with α-1,4 bonds.
Cellulose joins glucose with β-1,4 bonds.
Human amylase cuts α bonds only.
Cattle need microbes with cellulase to cut β bonds.

traps.A: Both are glucose polymers. Cellulose is not made of fructose.
traps.B: Cellulose has glycosidic bonds. They are β-1,4 instead of α-1,4.
traps.C: Water attraction is not the issue. The bond type is.
traps.D: Both use D-glucose. The difference is the α versus β link.

check.q: Which glucose polymer stores energy in animals?
check.a: Glycogen, with α-1,4 and α-1,6 bonds.

explain.answer: Phospholipids are amphipathic: a polar head and two nonpolar tails.

trick.text: Polar heads out, nonpolar tails in.

steps: The phosphate head is polar and **hydrophilic**.
The two fatty-acid tails are nonpolar and hydrophobic.
Heads face the water; tails hide from it.
Two layers do this together: a bilayer.

traps.A: If every part were hydrophobic, no head group would face the water.
traps.C: No covalent bonds form with water. Tails cluster away from it.
traps.D: Fatty-acid tails are nonpolar. They carry no partial negative charge.
traps.E: Ester hydrolysis would break the lipid apart, not organize a bilayer.

check.q: In a micelle, do the tails point in or out?

explain.answer: Primary structure survives: heat does not break peptide bonds.

trick.text: Heat breaks weak bonds, not peptide bonds.

steps: Same mass and sequence: the **peptide bonds** are intact.
Primary structure is that covalent sequence.
Higher levels rely mostly on weak non-covalent forces.
Heat breaks those forces, so the fold and activity are lost.

traps.A: Helices and sheets are held by hydrogen bonds, not covalent bonds.
traps.B: The fold relies mostly on weak bonds; disulfides are only part of it.
traps.D: Subunit contacts are non-covalent, so heat disrupts them too.
traps.E: Heat disrupts every higher level, not only secondary structure.

check.q: Which bond defines primary structure?
check.a: The peptide bond between amino acids.

explain.answer: Uracil in the RNA template pairs with adenine.
steps: RNA uses **uracil** in place of thymine.
Adenine pairs with thymine in DNA, uracil in RNA.
The template here is RNA, so the partner is U.

traps.A: Thymine is a DNA base. The template is RNA, which carries uracil.
traps.B: Guanine pairs with cytosine, not with adenine.
traps.C: Cytosine pairs with guanine, never with adenine.
traps.D: Inosine is a tRNA wobble base, not an mRNA template base.

check.q: In DNA, which base pairs with adenine?

explain.answer: X is competitive: Vmax is unchanged and the apparent Km rises.
steps: More substrate restores **Vmax**: the inhibitor is outcompeted.
Km doubled: more substrate is needed for half Vmax.
The plots meet on the y-axis, at 1/Vmax.
Same Vmax with a higher Km means competitive.

traps.A: Non-competitive lowers Vmax and leaves Km unchanged.
traps.C: Uncompetitive lowers both Vmax and Km.
traps.D: Mixed inhibition lowers Vmax as well as shifting Km.
traps.E: An activator speeds the enzyme up. Km would not double.

check.q: Which inhibitor lowers Vmax but leaves Km alone?

explain.answer: Only eukaryotes have a membrane-bound nucleus and organelles.
steps: Both cell types have ribosomes, membrane, DNA, cytoplasm.
Prokaryotes keep DNA in a **nucleoid**, with no membrane.
Eukaryotes wrap DNA in a nuclear envelope.
They also have organelles like mitochondria and Golgi.

traps.A: Prokaryotes have ribosomes too; theirs are smaller, 70S.
traps.C: Every cell has a plasma membrane.
traps.D: Both cell types store their genes in DNA.
traps.E: All cells have cytoplasm with proteins and metabolites.

check.q: Do bacteria have mitochondria?
check.a: No. They have no membrane-bound organelles.

explain.answer: The Golgi apparatus modifies, sorts and packages secreted proteins.

trick.text: ER makes it, Golgi ships it.

steps: Rough ER makes and folds the protein first.
Vesicles carry it to the **Golgi apparatus**.
The Golgi adds sugars and other tags.
It sorts the protein into vesicles for the membrane.

traps.A: Rough ER comes first: synthesis and folding, not final sorting.
traps.B: Smooth ER makes lipids and detoxifies. It does not sort secretions.
traps.C: Lysosomes digest material. They do not package secreted proteins.
traps.D: Peroxisomes break down fatty acids and hydrogen peroxide.

check.q: Where does a secreted protein go first after translation?

explain.answer: In 5% saline, red cells lose water and shrink (crenation).
steps: 5% NaCl holds more solute than the cell: **hypertonic**.
Water moves toward the higher solute by osmosis.
Water leaves the cell, so the cell shrinks.
Shrunken red cells look spiky: crenation.

traps.A: Swelling and lysis happen in hypotonic solution, the opposite case.
traps.B: Red cells react fast to tonicity; they have no cell wall.
traps.C: The cell does not pump NaCl in to match. Water moves instead.
traps.D: Apoptosis is programmed cell death, not a 30 second osmotic change.

check.q: What happens to red cells in pure water?

explain.answer: The product is (S)-2-butanol, made by SN2 with inversion.

trick.text: Second order and backside attack: SN2 inverts.

steps: Rate = k[substrate][NaOH]: second order means **SN2**.
DMSO is polar aprotic, which favors SN2.
Hydroxide attacks from the back side of C2.
Backside attack inverts the center: R becomes S.

traps.A: SN1 is first order. This rate depends on both reactants.
traps.B: Racemizing needs a carbocation (SN1). The second-order rate rules it out.
traps.C: The product is an alcohol, not an alkene.
traps.D: SN2 never gives retention. Backside attack inverts the center.

check.q: What is the rate law for SN1?

explain.answer: They are the same meso compound: achiral and optically inactive.
steps: Two stereocenters with opposite labels: (2R,3S).
Matching ends give a **mirror plane** between C2 and C3.
A molecule with an internal mirror plane is meso.
Its mirror image is itself: achiral, optically inactive.

traps.A: Enantiomers are non-superimposable. This mirror image superimposes.
traps.B: Diastereomers are different compounds. These two are one molecule.
traps.D: The connectivity is identical, so they are not constitutional isomers.
traps.E: Conformers are shapes of one compound. The key here is the mirror plane.

check.q: Is (2R,3R)-2,3-dichlorobutane meso?
check.a: No. It is chiral, and (2S,3S) is its enantiomer.

explain.answer: The diene must be s-cis so both ends bond to the dienophile at once.
steps: Diels-Alder is one **concerted** [4+2] step.
Both diene ends must reach the dienophile together.
s-cis puts C1 and C4 on the same side.
s-trans holds the two ends too far apart.

traps.A: s-trans is the problem: its ends point apart and cannot both bond.
traps.C: Only s-cis reacts. A diene locked s-trans does not.
traps.D: Anti-periplanar is an E2 requirement, not a Diels-Alder one.
traps.E: Eclipsed describes bond rotation, not the s-cis diene shape.

check.q: Why is cyclopentadiene such a reactive diene?

explain.answer: Lindlar adds H2 once, syn, giving cis-2-butene.
steps: Lindlar is **poisoned** palladium: it stops at the alkene.
Both H atoms add to the same face: syn.
Syn addition to 2-butyne gives cis-2-butene.

traps.A: Trans alkenes come from Na in liquid NH3, an anti route.
traps.B: Over-reduction to butane happens on plain Pd/C, not Lindlar.
traps.C: No isomerization: the double bond stays at C2.
traps.E: Hydrogenation only adds H atoms. It cannot make a diene here.

check.q: What does Na in liquid NH3 make from 2-butyne?

explain.answer: Cyclobutadiene is anti-aromatic: less stable than its open chain.
steps: Check the ring: cyclic, planar, fully **conjugated**.
Count the pi electrons: 4.
4 fits 4n with n = 1, not 4n + 2.
4n in a planar ring means anti-aromatic: destabilized.

traps.A: Aromatic with n = 1 needs 6 pi electrons (4n + 2). It has 4.
traps.C: Non-aromatic means not planar or not conjugated. This ring is both.
traps.D: Aromaticity follows the electron count, not the temperature.
traps.E: Pseudo-aromatic is not a Hückel class. The count gives anti-aromatic.

check.q: How many pi electrons does benzene have?

explain.answer: Methoxide attacks the less-substituted carbon, by SN2.

trick.text: Base opens epoxides at the less hindered carbon.

steps: Basic conditions: the epoxide oxygen is not **protonated**.
No carbocation character, so sterics decide.
Methoxide attacks the less hindered carbon from the back.
The ring opens; the alkoxide then picks up a proton.

traps.A: SN2 is sensitive to sterics, so there is a clear preference.
traps.C: The strained three-membered ring opens readily with strong nucleophiles.
traps.D: The more-substituted carbon wins under acid, not under base.
traps.E: The epoxide oxygen leaves. Methoxide bonds to a ring carbon.

check.q: Under acid, which epoxide carbon is attacked?

explain.answer: Two ethanols add to the carbonyl carbon: the product is an acetal.

trick.text: Remove the water to drive it to the acetal.

steps: The first ethanol adds to give a **hemiacetal**.
Acid protonates the OH, which leaves as water.
The second ethanol adds to that same carbon.
Dean-Stark removes water, pushing it to the acetal.

traps.A: A hemiacetal is the midpoint. Removing water drives it on to the acetal.
traps.B: A simple ether has one OR. This carbon ends with two.
traps.D: An ester needs a carboxylic acid or derivative, not an aldehyde.
traps.E: An enol ether needs a C=C. This carbon holds two OR groups.

check.q: What turns an acetal back into the aldehyde?

explain.answer: The carboxylate spreads its charge over two oxygens by resonance.
steps: Acidity tracks **conjugate base** stability.
Carboxylate: charge shared by two equal oxygens.
Alkoxide: charge stuck on one oxygen.
Spread charge is more stable, so the acid is stronger.

traps.A: Induction helps, but it is small next to resonance.
traps.C: A stronger O-H bond would make the acid weaker, not stronger.
traps.D: The alpha C-H is not the proton lost. The O-H proton is.
traps.E: Hydrogen bonds that stabilize the acid would lower its acidity.

check.q: Which is more acidic, phenol or ethanol?
check.a: Phenol: its anion is resonance stabilized.

explain.answer: Bulky base and leaving group give the less-substituted (Hofmann) alkene.
steps: The leaving group is bulky: **trimethylamine**.
Heated hydroxide removes a beta hydrogen in an E2.
The bulk blocks the inner, crowded hydrogens.
The most open hydrogen goes: less-substituted alkene.

traps.B: More-substituted is the Zaitsev result. Hofmann gives the opposite.
traps.C: H2SO4 with heat is alcohol dehydration, not Hofmann elimination.
traps.D: A heated quaternary ammonium hydroxide eliminates; it does not substitute.
traps.E: Hofmann elimination is an ionic E2, not a radical process.

check.q: Zaitsev or Hofmann: which gives the more-substituted alkene?

explain.answer: p-Xylene has 3 carbon environments; o-xylene has 4.
steps: Group carbons that a **symmetry** move swaps.
p-Xylene: 2 ring types plus 1 methyl type = 3.
o-Xylene: one mirror plane through the ring.
o-Xylene: 3 ring types plus 1 methyl type = 4.

traps.A: Both molecules have symmetry, so equivalent carbons share a signal.
traps.C: Both counts are too high: symmetry pairs carbons, giving 3 and 4.
traps.D: Each count leaves out the methyl carbons, their own signal.
traps.E: o-Xylene has a mirror plane, so its carbons pair up: 4, not 8.

check.q: How many carbon-13 signals does benzene give?
check.a: One: all six carbons are equivalent.
